title: Patients with additional needs
blurb: Physical disability, learning disability, autism, dementia and sensory loss: the reasonable adjustments that make care accessible, including domiciliary visits.
question: A wheelchair user who is also hard of hearing arrives with her carer for a check-up. The carer starts answering every question for her. How should you communicate with her, and how do you find out how she would like to get into the dental chair?

teach.body: A patient has additional needs when a physical, sensory, learning, cognitive or mental health condition affects how they access or cope with dental care. The Equality Act 2010 requires practices to make reasonable adjustments so disabled people are not put at a disadvantage. The aim is not to treat everyone the same. It is to give everyone the same chance of good care. The golden rule: ask the patient what helps them, and never assume.

teach.caption: Many patients have more than one need, and needs can change over time, so update the record at every visit.

head: Need
Reasonable adjustments
rows: Ground-floor surgery, ramp; ask how they transfer
Face them, speak clearly, hearing loop, BSL interpreter
Say who you are, describe each step, offer your arm
Easy-read information, longer slots, involve them
Quiet times, little waiting, warn about noises
Short early visits, same team, pause and reassure

teach.body: A patient with a physical disability is the expert on their own body. Ask how they usually transfer and what help they want. Some prefer to be treated in their own wheelchair, some transfer independently and some need a hoist, which only trained staff should use. Never push someone's wheelchair or touch a guide dog without asking. Talk to the patient, not their carer: carers give valuable help, but the patient is the one being treated, and adults must be presumed to have capacity.

teach.caption: Lip-readers need to see your mouth, in good light, without a mask. Have the conversation before treatment starts, then agree simple signals for use during it.

teach.body: Give information in a way the person can understand, such as easy-read leaflets or pictures, and involve them in decisions. A familiarisation visit to see the surgery can help. For autistic patients, book quieter times, keep waiting short and warn before noises, lights or touch. People with dementia cope best with short, early appointments and familiar faces. If they become distressed, pause and reassure. Capacity can fluctuate, so it is assessed for each decision. NHS services must also meet the Accessible Information Standard.

teach.caption: Complex cases that cannot be managed in practice or at home may be referred to special care dentistry, often provided by the Community Dental Service.

teach.text: Don't talk over the patient to their carer, interpreter or family member. Address the patient directly, presume they have capacity, and only turn to best-interests decisions if a capacity assessment shows they lack it.

items: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010, not a favour.
Ask the patient what helps, especially how they transfer from a wheelchair.
Hearing loss: face them, speak clearly at a normal pace. Sight loss: introduce yourself and describe each step.
Learning disability: accessible information and involvement. Autism: quiet, short waits. Dementia: short visits, pause and reassure.
Domiciliary care brings treatment to housebound patients after a risk assessment.

summary: You can now describe the main kinds of additional need, choose reasonable adjustments for physical, sensory, learning and cognitive needs, communicate directly with the patient rather than their carer, and explain how domiciliary and special care services reach patients who cannot attend a practice.

A.q: A patient who uses a wheelchair asks how they will get into the dental chair. What is the best approach?
options: Lift them across with a colleague
Treat them in the wheelchair anyway
Ask how they usually transfer and what help they need
Explain that the practice cannot treat wheelchair users
A.why: The patient knows their own needs best. Asking how they usually transfer keeps them safe and respects their independence.

whyNot.0: Lifting a patient manually without asking risks injury to them and to staff.
whyNot.1: Some patients prefer this, but you should ask rather than decide for them.
whyNot.3: Refusing care instead of making reasonable adjustments could breach the Equality Act 2010.

A.q: A patient who is deaf and lip-reads attends alone. Which action best supports communication?
options: Face her and speak clearly at a normal pace
Speak loudly from behind the chair
Exaggerate each word very slowly
Write everything down and avoid speaking at all
A.why: Lip-readers need to see your face clearly, so face the patient and speak naturally at a normal pace.

whyNot.1: She cannot lip-read from behind, and shouting distorts lip patterns.
whyNot.2: Exaggerated mouth movements make lip-reading harder, not easier.
whyNot.3: Writing can help alongside speech, but she has not asked you to stop talking.

A.q: A patient living with dementia becomes confused and distressed during a long appointment. What is most appropriate?
options: Finish quickly while he is still seated
Ask his carer to take him out to calm down
Carry on, but explain each step more loudly to him
Pause, reassure him and plan shorter visits
A.why: Pausing and reassuring helps him settle, and shorter appointments in future reduce the chance of distress.

whyNot.0: Rushing a distressed patient is unsafe and ignores his needs.
whyNot.1: Sending him out passes the problem on rather than supporting him.
whyNot.2: Raising your voice can increase confusion and distress.

B.q: A patient who is blind attends for treatment. Which approach best supports her?
options: Guide her by pushing gently from behind
Describe the room and explain each step
Keep talking to a minimum to avoid confusion
Ask her guide dog to wait at reception
B.why: Describing the surroundings and explaining each step before it happens removes surprises and helps her feel safe.

whyNot.0: Offer your arm for her to hold instead; pushing someone is disorientating.
whyNot.2: She relies on spoken information, so less talking increases uncertainty.
whyNot.3: Guide dogs are generally welcome; decide together where the dog waits rather than separating them by default.

B.q: An autistic patient's parent says waiting rooms are overwhelming for him. Which adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Book a quieter time and keep waiting short
Ask him to wait in the car park until called
Double the appointment length as standard
Refer him to hospital for all future care
B.why: Quieter appointment times and minimal waiting reduce sensory overload, which is a simple, reasonable adjustment.

whyNot.1: Making him wait outside is not a planned adjustment and may be unsafe.
whyNot.2: Longer appointments may help some patients, but they don't address a busy waiting room.
whyNot.3: Most autistic patients can be treated in practice with adjustments; referral is not automatic.

B.q: Which statement about domiciliary dental care is correct?
options: It is only for patients over 80
Any treatment can be done at home
It needs no special risk assessment beforehand
It brings care to housebound people
B.why: Domiciliary care treats patients who cannot attend a practice, at home or in a care home, after a risk assessment.

whyNot.0: There is no age rule; it is based on being unable to attend a practice.
whyNot.1: Treatment at home is limited by equipment and safety, so complex care is referred.
whyNot.2: A risk assessment covering medical history, access and lone working is essential.

C.q: A patient with a learning disability attends an examination and seems anxious. What is most appropriate?
options: Explain everything to the carer only
Proceed quickly to keep the visit short
Use accessible information and involve him
Ask the carer to sign the consent form for him
C.why: Information he can understand, such as simple words or pictures, lets him take part in decisions about his own care.

whyNot.0: The patient should be involved and addressed directly, not bypassed.
whyNot.1: Rushing increases anxiety and leaves no time for him to understand.
whyNot.3: Adults are presumed to have capacity; a carer cannot simply sign on their behalf.

C.q: A patient's carer keeps answering the dentist's questions for him. What should you do?
options: Let the carer answer, since it saves time
Speak to the patient directly, including him
Ask the carer to leave the surgery for a while
Record the carer as his decision-maker
C.why: The patient should be addressed directly and given the chance to answer, with the carer supporting rather than replacing him.

whyNot.0: Letting the carer answer everything excludes the patient from his own care.
whyNot.2: Carers often provide valuable support; removing them is not the first step.
whyNot.3: A carer is not automatically a decision-maker; capacity is presumed unless assessed otherwise.

C.q: Which is NOT a reasonable adjustment for a patient with hearing loss?
options: Using a hearing loop at reception
Booking a BSL interpreter
Lowering your mask to talk when safe
Speaking loudly from across the room
C.why: Shouting from a distance distorts speech and hides your face, so it does not help someone with hearing loss.

whyNot.0: A hearing loop helps hearing-aid users pick up speech clearly.
whyNot.1: A BSL interpreter supports patients whose first language is British Sign Language.
whyNot.2: Lowering your mask when it is safe lets lip-readers see your mouth.

reteach.title: Remove the barrier, not the patient
reteach.question: Picture three patients who can't get through the same door: one in a wheelchair, one who can't read the sign, one overwhelmed by the noise. What does the practice change?

blocks.body: It helps to see disability as a mismatch between a person and their surroundings. Steps are a barrier to a wheelchair user, small print is a barrier to someone with sight loss, and a busy waiting room is a barrier to an autistic person. A reasonable adjustment removes the barrier: a ramp or ground-floor surgery, large print or a spoken explanation, a quiet appointment time. And the quickest way to find the barrier is to ask the patient.

head: Barrier
Adjustment
rows: Face them, mask down to talk

explain.body: Ask how the patient usually transfers and what help they want. Some stay in their wheelchair, some transfer independently, some need a hoist used only by trained staff. Never move a wheelchair without asking.

steps.label: Agree
steps.sub: Their method, and what help they want

test.q: Before helping a wheelchair user into the dental chair, what should you do first?
options: Apply the brakes and lift them
Ask how they prefer to transfer
Call a colleague to use the hoist
Recline the chair fully flat
test.why: Asking first respects their independence and means you use the method that is safest for them.

whyNot.0: Lifting without asking is unsafe and disrespectful.
whyNot.2: A hoist may not be needed; ask before choosing equipment.
whyNot.3: Chair position comes after agreeing how they will transfer.

explain.body: For hearing loss, face the patient, speak clearly at a normal pace, lower your mask to talk when safe, and use a hearing loop or BSL interpreter. For sight loss, say who you are, describe the room and each step, and offer your arm.

test.q: How should you guide a blind patient from reception to the surgery?
options: Push them gently by the shoulders
Walk ahead and call back to them
Offer your arm for them to hold
Ask their companion to lead them
test.why: Offering your arm lets the patient hold on and follow your movement, which is safe and respectful.

whyNot.0: Pushing is disorientating and removes their control.
whyNot.1: Calling from ahead gives no physical guidance around obstacles.
whyNot.3: They may come alone; offer your own support first.

explain.body: Use accessible information and involve the patient in decisions. Book quieter times and limit waiting for autistic patients. For dementia, keep visits short and early with familiar staff, and pause to reassure if they become distressed. Capacity is assessed per decision.

test.q: Which appointment plan best suits a patient with dementia?
options: A short appointment early in the day
A long session to finish everything
The last slot before the practice closes
A different clinician at each visit
test.why: Short, early appointments suit people with dementia, who often tire and become more confused later in the day.

whyNot.1: Long sessions increase the risk of confusion and distress.
whyNot.2: Late-day slots are often harder for people with dementia.
whyNot.3: Familiar faces help; changing clinicians increases confusion.

explain.body: Domiciliary visits bring treatment to patients who cannot attend a practice, at home or in a care home. They need a risk assessment, portable equipment, emergency drugs and IPC supplies. Complex care is referred, often to the Community Dental Service.

items.label: or care home: where treatment happens
complex care to special care dentistry

test.q: Who is domiciliary dental care mainly for?
options: Patients who prefer not to travel
Patients unable to attend a practice
Any patient over retirement age
Patients still waiting for an NHS dentist place
test.why: Domiciliary care is for people who cannot reasonably attend a practice, such as housebound patients or care home residents.

whyNot.0: Preference alone is not the reason for a domiciliary visit.
whyNot.2: Age is not a criterion; inability to attend is.
whyNot.3: Waiting lists are a separate issue; domiciliary care is about access needs.
